specPoints.text: describe the stages in the carbon cycle, including respiration, photosynthesis, decomposition and combustion

primer.text: Carbon is the backbone of every living molecule, and the carbon cycle tracks where it travels. This note follows carbon from the air into plants by photosynthesis, along food chains through feeding, and back into the atmosphere through respiration, decomposition and combustion.

lessons.title: Cycling Carbon Through Ecosystems
sourceHeadings: Uptake of carbon by living organisms
lessons.opening: Carbon sits at the centre of every biological molecule, and plants constantly pull carbon dioxide out of the air to build the glucose that becomes their biomass, so the element keeps flowing through every ecosystem.
keyPoints: Carbon forms part of the biological molecules that build cells, such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
Plants take carbon dioxide out of the air during photosynthesis.
The carbon captured becomes glucose, which plants turn into carbohydrates, fats and proteins in their biomass.

low.restatement: Green plants soak up carbon dioxide and lock the carbon into their own bodies.
low.analogy: A factory taking in raw material from the air and storing it as product stock.
low.examPointer: Quote photosynthesis as the uptake step and name glucose plus biomass as the products.

medium.restatement: Photosynthesis is the door through which carbon enters the living world: carbon dioxide goes in, glucose is assembled, and that glucose is rebuilt into the carbohydrates, fats and proteins that make up plant biomass.
medium.analogy: Plants are carbon importers — the atmosphere is the warehouse and their biomass is the shelf where the stock lands.
medium.examPointer: If asked where carbon enters the cycle, name photosynthesis and follow the carbon into glucose and then biomass.

check.stem: In which form do plants take carbon out of the atmosphere?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: As glucose ready-made by the air
options.explanation: The air never carries glucose; plants assemble it themselves.
Rocks store carbon but plants cannot absorb them directly.
Methane is not what plants absorb during photosynthesis.

check.stem: Which process captures carbon dioxide and builds glucose in plant cells?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Respiration, which burns glucose for energy
options.explanation: Respiration releases carbon dioxide; it never builds glucose.
Decomposers recycle dead material; they do not assemble glucose in plant cells.
Combustion burns carbon stores; it cannot build glucose.

check.stem: What does a plant make from the glucose produced during photosynthesis?

options.text: Carbohydrates, fats and proteins that form its biomass
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Oxygen is a by-product, not the biomass material.
Nitrogen compounds are not built from glucose.
Minerals come from the soil, not from glucose.

check.stem: Why is carbon described as essential for living cells?

options.text: Because carbon forms part of the biological molecules that build cells, such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Warmth is not what carbon provides here.
Colour plays no role in the requirement.
Energy release involves respiration of food, not carbon alone.

check.stem: A wheat crop grows larger over summer. Where did most of its new carbon come from?

options.text: From carbon dioxide taken in from the air during photosynthesis
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: From minerals absorbed by the roots
options.explanation: Minerals add nutrients but supply no carbon.

options.text: From water taken up by the roots
options.explanation: Water provides hydrogen and oxygen, not the carbon bulk.

options.text: From the soil where seeds were buried
options.explanation: Soil is not the carbon source; the air is.

check.stem: State the process by which plants take carbon dioxide out of the air.
check.modelAnswer: Photosynthesis absorbs carbon dioxide and builds glucose inside plant cells.

check.stem: Name the molecule that plants convert into carbohydrates, fats and proteins.
check.modelAnswer: Glucose made during photosynthesis is converted into carbohydrates, fats and proteins.

check.stem: Explain why plants are described as the entry point for carbon into living ecosystems.
check.modelAnswer: Plants are the entry point because photosynthesis pulls carbon dioxide from the air into glucose, so every other organism gains carbon by feeding on plants or on creatures that fed on plants.

check.stem: A farmer seals a greenhouse and raises carbon dioxide levels. Predict the effect on plant biomass and explain why.
check.modelAnswer: Biomass should rise because extra carbon dioxide lets photosynthesis build more glucose, which the plants convert into carbohydrates, fats and proteins.

lessons.title: Putting Carbon Back into the Air
sourceHeadings: Transfer of carbon between living organisms
Release of carbon into the atmosphere
lessons.opening: Feeding moves carbon from plants into animals and up the food chain, while respiration, decomposition and combustion each push carbon dioxide back into the air, closing the carbon loop.
keyPoints: Herbivores take in carbon when they feed on plants, and carnivores gain it by eating other animals.
Respiration in plants and animals releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down dead material and waste, releasing carbon dioxide.
Dead remains can become fossil fuels, and burning them by combustion returns carbon dioxide to the air.

low.restatement: Eating spreads carbon through the chain; breathing, rotting and burning send it home.
low.analogy: A relay race where the baton is handed on by feeders and thrown back by three different runners.
low.examPointer: Name all three release routes — respiration, decomposition and combustion — when tracing carbon back to the air.

medium.restatement: Carbon rides the food chain inside digested molecules, then leaves living bodies through respiration; decomposers finish off dead matter the same way, and any carbon buried into fossil fuels rejoins the atmosphere when combustion burns it.
medium.analogy: A library book passed reader to reader until it is finally returned to the shelf by three separate couriers.
medium.examPointer: Examiners want the full loop, so pair every transfer route with its release route in the same answer.

check.stem: How does carbon move from a plant into a herbivore?

options.text: The herbivore feeds on the plant and digests its carbon compounds
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The herbivore breathes in carbon from the plant
options.explanation: Breathing takes in oxygen, not carbon from another organism.

options.text: Carbon drifts into animals through the soil
options.explanation: Soil does not pass carbon directly into animal bodies.

options.text: The plant injects carbon into animals through roots
options.explanation: Roots take up water and minerals; they do not transfer carbon to animals.

check.stem: Which process returns carbon dioxide to the air inside both plants and animals?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Photosynthesis absorbs carbon dioxide; it does not release it.
Nitrogen fixation handles nitrogen, not carbon dioxide.
Transpiration releases water vapour, not carbon dioxide.

check.stem: What role do bacteria and fungi play in the release of carbon from dead material?

options.text: They respire while breaking down dead and waste material during decomposition
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: They fix carbon dioxide into new glucose
options.explanation: Bacteria and fungi do not build glucose from air during decomposition.

options.text: They burn the material in small flames
options.explanation: No flames are involved; microbes release carbon dioxide by respiration.

options.text: They lock carbon permanently into rocks
options.explanation: Rocks are not made by decomposers in this cycle.

check.stem: How can carbon from a long-dead organism rejoin the atmosphere?

options.text: Its remains form fossil fuels, and combustion of those fuels releases carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Carbon is conserved; it re-enters the air when fuels burn.

options.text: Rain dissolves its carbon into clouds
options.explanation: Clouds are not the route; burning fossil fuels is.
Dead remains are not breathed out; they are buried and burned over time.

check.stem: A forest fire sweeps through dead wood on the ground. Which carbon-release process does this match?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Fire does not build glucose.
Nitrification is a soil nitrogen process, not a carbon release.
Egestion removes faeces; it is not a burning process.

check.stem: Name the process in which microorganisms break down dead material and release carbon dioxide.
check.modelAnswer: Decomposition, carried out by bacteria and fungi, breaks down dead material and releases carbon dioxide by respiration.

check.stem: State the process that releases carbon dioxide when fossil fuels are burned.
check.modelAnswer: Combustion of fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.

check.stem: Explain why respiration and photosynthesis act as opposite arrows in the carbon cycle.
check.modelAnswer: Respiration releases carbon dioxide into the air while photosynthesis removes it, so the two processes push carbon in opposite directions.

check.stem: A wetland is drained and its buried plant remains are later burned in a power station. Trace the carbon.
check.modelAnswer: Buried plant remains became fossil fuels, and burning them by combustion releases the stored carbon back into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide.

glossary.definition: The process in which plants absorb carbon dioxide from the air and build glucose inside their cells.
The living matter of an organism, built from carbohydrates, fats and proteins.
The process in living organisms that releases energy from food and returns carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
The breakdown of dead material and waste by microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi.
The burning of fuels such as fossil fuels, which releases carbon dioxide into the air.
